name: Māori
variety: Modern standard Māori of the North Island. The conservative reference is the speech of elders born between the 1880s and the 1930s (MAONZE corpus); changes in younger speakers are noted
sources: Harlow, Ray (2007). Māori: A Linguistic Introduction. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
Biggs, Bruce (1961). The structure of New Zealand Maaori. Anthropological Linguistics 3(3).

Watson, Catherine I., Maclagan, Margaret A., King, Jeanette, Harlow, Ray & Keegan, Peter J. (2016). Sound change in Māori and the influence of New Zealand English. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 46(2), 185-218.
Maclagan, Margaret & King, Jeanette (2007). Aspiration of plosives in Māori: change over time. Australian Journal of Linguistics 27(1), 81-96.
Maclagan, Margaret & King, Jeanette (2002). The pronunciation of wh in Māori: a case study from the late nineteenth century. Te Reo 45.

King, Jeanette, Harlow, Ray, Watson, Catherine, Keegan, Peter & Maclagan, Margaret (2009). Changing pronunciation of the Māori language: implications for revitalization. In J. Reyhner & L. Lockard (eds.), Indigenous Language Revitalization, 85-96. Flagstaff: Northern Arizona University.
Maclagan, Margaret and others (2009). Investigating changes in the rhythm of Māori over time. Proceedings of Interspeech 2009, Brighton.
contrasts: short versus long vowels: keke 'cake' versus kēkē 'armpit', matua 'parent' versus mātua 'parents', kaka 'garment' versus kākā 'parrot' versus kakā 'hot'
diphthongs that differ only in the height of the second element (ai versus ae, au versus ao) or of the first (ou versus au)
velar nasal ŋ in all positions, including word-initially (ngā)
f (written wh) versus h versus w
ten consonants only; no voicing contrast, no sibilants
no glottal stop phoneme in the standard language, unlike Hawaiian; vowels that meet form a long vowel, a diphthong or a hiatus
allophony: /t/ is affricated before /i/ and /u/, most clearly at the end of a phrase

/p t k/ were unaspirated for speakers born in the nineteenth century and are now usually aspirated: a speaker born in 1885 aspirated 6 percent of stops, one born in 1972 aspirated 88 percent (Maclagan & King 2007)
/f/ was mostly bilabial [ɸ] for speakers born in the nineteenth century, with [ʍ], [h] and [f] as variants; it is now labiodental [f]
/ɾ/ is an alveolar tap, an approximant in fast speech
in the Whanganui and Taranaki dialects /h/ is a glottal stop and wh is [ʔw]; South Island dialects have k for ŋ, and Tūhoe and the eastern Bay of Plenty have n for ŋ
/u uː/ are fronted towards [ʉ], first after /t/ and generally for younger speakers; /e eː/ are raised for younger speakers
short /a/ is central and closer than long /aː/; for the oldest speakers every long vowel is more peripheral than its short partner
for younger speakers ai and ae, and au and ou, are merging, and the length contrast of all pairs except a and ā is weakened
syllable_structure: (C)V, where V is a short vowel, a long vowel or a diphthong; no codas and no consonant clusters
phonotactics: every consonant is followed by a vowel; all words end in a vowel
wo, wu, who, whu do not occur in native words
a short vowel with its preceding consonant counts as one mora; long vowels and diphthongs count as two

stress.rule: Stress falls on the first long vowel of the word; if there is none, on the first diphthong that is not word-final; otherwise on the first syllable; it lies no further back than the fourth mora from the end. In the last phrase of a sentence the phrase stress falls on the penultimate mora.
stress.cues: pitch and duration; younger speakers tend to lengthen the stressed first syllable of three-syllable words

rhythm.notes: Māori is conventionally described as mora-timed; King et al. (2009) report a drift towards syllable timing and perhaps stress timing in younger speakers. Maclagan and others (2009) found that PVI measures did not capture the change, so no nPVI is given. Final lengthening has not been measured in the sources consulted; the value is a default.

length.notes: Short vowels last a little over 60 ms in running speech in all generations. For speakers born in the 1880s long vowels were about twice as long; the ratio has shrunk since, least for a and ā (King et al. 2009). Long vowels are written with a macron and behave as two like vowels in one morpheme.

intonation.declarative: pitch peak on the stressed syllable of each phrase and an overall fall to low at the end
intonation.yes_no_question: same wording as a statement; marked by a rise at the end
intonation.wh_question: the question word (aha, wai, hea) carries the phrase stress; final fall
intonation.continuation: non-final phrases end without the final fall
intonation.accent_shape: high pitch on the stressed mora followed by a fall
intonation.notes: After the auditory descriptions in Bauer (1993) and Harlow (2007); instrumental work on Māori intonation is scarce.

problems: stress is always put on the penultimate syllable (the engine default); the Māori rule of first long vowel, else first diphthong, else first syllable is not implemented, so Māori, whānau, tangata, wahine, aroha, mātua all get the wrong stress
ae and ai are both pronounced [aɪ], so the contrast that conservative speakers keep (tae versus tai) is lost; ao is given the quality of English [aʊ]
oe is pronounced [we]: koe comes out as [kwe], hoe as [hwe]
short a has the same quality as long ā
the voice file inserts a short pause after every word (words 1 2), which breaks up the phrase rhythm
numbers are disabled in the engine; the word list has only the digits 0 to 9
/t/ is not affricated before i and u
good: long vowels are twice as long as short ones (280 against 140 units)
u is a fronted [ʉ], as in present-day speech
wh is [f] and ng is [ŋ] in all positions

notes: Watson et al. (2016) report F1 and F2 for 31 men and 31 women in three generations; I could not check their tables and give no formant block.
